response.sql:
WITH line_totals AS (
  SELECT b.budget_id,
         COALESCE(SUM(e.cost), 0) AS total,
         COUNT(e.expense_id) AS n
  FROM budget b
  LEFT JOIN expense e ON e.link_to_budget = b.budget_id
  GROUP BY b.budget_id
),
avg_total AS (
  SELECT AVG(total) AS avg_total FROM line_totals
),
above AS (
  SELECT lt.total, lt.n, at.avg_total
  FROM line_totals lt
  CROSS JOIN avg_total at
  WHERE lt.total > at.avg_total
)
SELECT AVG(total) AS avg_above_total,
       SUM(n) AS total_expenses,
       AVG(total - avg_total) AS avg_excess_over_average
FROM above;

assumptions.assumption: Every expense row counts toward its budget line, regardless of its `approved` value, because the request does not mention approval status.
"Above that average" means strictly greater than the average of per-line totals.
Budget lines with no expenses get a total of 0 and a count of 0 via LEFT JOIN and COALESCE, and they are included in the average, as the request specifies.
Expense rows are counted by `expense_id`, so an expense with a NULL cost still counts as an expense while contributing nothing to the total.

alternatives.interpretation: Only approved expenses count toward each budget line's total and expense count. Lines with no approved expenses are still included in the average as 0.
alternatives.sql:
WITH line_totals AS (
  SELECT b.budget_id,
         COALESCE(SUM(e.cost), 0) AS total,
         COUNT(e.expense_id) AS n
  FROM budget b
  LEFT JOIN expense e ON e.link_to_budget = b.budget_id AND e.approved = 'true'
  GROUP BY b.budget_id
),
avg_total AS (
  SELECT AVG(total) AS avg_total FROM line_totals
),
above AS (
  SELECT lt.total, lt.n, at.avg_total
  FROM line_totals lt
  CROSS JOIN avg_total at
  WHERE lt.total > at.avg_total
)
SELECT AVG(total) AS avg_above_total,
       SUM(n) AS total_expenses,
       AVG(total - avg_total) AS avg_excess_over_average
FROM above;
